solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Neat small tool plus second utensil (5,3,4)

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a pick is a digging tool
plus = and
S is the abbreviation for second
a pan is a kitchen utensil

annotation.surface: An inventory of a tidy toolkit: a little tool, then a kitchen utensil.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Small tool' reads as one item, but the setter splits it into S and PICK; the enumeration (5,3,4) shows the answer is a phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: A fixed idiom for a spotlessly clean and tidy room, a plain synonym of neat.

entries.clue: Take action against core set-up that goes wrong (9)

indicators.note: something that goes wrong ends up in a different order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A complaint about a central system that keeps failing and someone demanding it be dealt with.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'set-up' is ignored; its letters join CORE as fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: The legal sense: 'action' here is a lawsuit, bringing someone before a court.

entries.clue: Greens perhaps in parliament (7)

blocks.note: village greens are an example of open land shared by a community
the elected lower house of the UK Parliament

annotation.surface: A remark about the Green Party having members in parliament.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Greens' looks like the Green Party, which fits the parliament picture perfectly, but it means patches of shared grass. The House of Commons is the elected chamber of the British Parliament.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example for shared village land, then the usual short name for Britain's lower house.

entries.clue: Point the finger at copper in unusual case (6)

indicators.note: copper goes in the rearranged letters
the letters of case are put in an unusual order

blocks.note: first part of ACSE, an anagram of CASE
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
rest of ACSE

annotation.surface: Blaming a police officer in a strange criminal case.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Copper' pulls toward the police slang in the surface, but it is the metal, symbol Cu.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: pointing the finger is blaming someone, the gesture standing for the charge.

entries.clue: Padre condemned hanging (5)

definitions.note: hanging as a noun: a curtain or cloth hung up

indicators.note: something condemned is wrecked, so its letters are knocked about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters

annotation.surface: A priest sentenced to death by the rope.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'hanging' an execution, but it is a noun: a curtain or cloth hung up.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym once 'hanging' is read as a noun: a curtain or cloth hung at a window.

entries.clue: Bake Off item regularly taking prize (3)

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals: the 1st, 3rd and 5th

blocks.note: the 1st, 3rd and 5th letters of the word

annotation.surface: A baked entry on a television cookery contest winning an award.
annotation.walkthrough: The Great British Bake Off is a popular British television baking contest, where a pie is a standard bake.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a pastry dish is one of the bakes set on the television contest.

entries.clue: Word broken by Sunak on good nursing? (10)

indicators.note: the word is split open with Sunak's name inside
in a down clue, one thing on another comes after it

blocks.note: first part of NOUN, a word
Rishi Sunak, UK Prime Minister 2022–24
rest of NOUN
G is the abbreviation for good

annotation.surface: A politician's promise broken, with a jab about how well he looked after things.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Word' is a noun and the fodder is NOUN itself; Rishi Sunak was the British Prime Minister. The question mark flags the loose definition: nursing a baby is feeding it.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: nursing a baby means feeding it, and the question mark admits the stretch.

entries.clue: Structure in support of motorway (4)

blocks.note: for = in favour of
British motorways are numbered M1, M6 and so on

annotation.surface: An engineer's note about a bridge structure holding up a motorway.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as civil engineering, where 'support' is physical; here it means being in favour of something.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the shape or arrangement of a piece of writing or music.

entries.clue: Two cuppas you finally got in stately home (7)

indicators.note: take only the final letter of you

blocks.note: cha (or char) is British slang for tea
the second cup of tea
last letter of YOU

annotation.surface: A visitor to a grand house being served a couple of cups of tea.
annotation.walkthrough: A cuppa is a British cup of tea; the two cuppas are two different words for tea, CHA and TEA.
annotation.definitionFit: A French country house or castle, the counterpart of an English stately home.

entries.clue: Risky feel with journey (5,3,2)

blocks.note: feel = touch
with = and
go = travel, journey

annotation.surface: A nervous traveller's sense that the trip ahead is dangerous.
annotation.walkthrough: Each small word is translated in turn; 'with' becomes AND.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for a situation whose outcome is uncertain and could go badly.

entries.clue: Troublesome old emperor coming to US (7)

indicators.note: the pieces are joined up, one arriving at the next

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
Nero, the Roman emperor
used as it stands

annotation.surface: A difficult ancient ruler arriving on a trip to America.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old emperor' looks like one phrase for Nero, but 'old' is O on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a burdensome duty is a troublesome one.

entries.clue: Sense of dissatisfaction when nuisance is about (5)

indicators.note: the answer is about, that is present, in the words that precede it

blocks.note: whEN NUIsance

annotation.surface: Feeling fed up whenever an irritating person is around.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a complete little observation, so the answer sitting across 'when nuisance' is easy to read past.
annotation.definitionFit: A French loanword for listless boredom, the weary dissatisfaction of having nothing worth doing.

entries.clue: Modern athletics event and where it’s reported (9)

blocks.note: modern = new
a sprint is a short running race

annotation.surface: A newfangled track event and the newspaper page that covers it.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the wordplay: 'it' is the race, reported in the paper.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the cheap paper newspapers are printed on, where events get reported.

entries.clue: Holiday afloat for Tom? (6)

blocks.note: a pleasure voyage on a ship
the surname of Tom, the Hollywood film actor

annotation.surface: Someone asking whether a boat trip would suit a friend called Tom.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second definition as an example: Tom is one famous bearer of the surname.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain description of a sea holiday, then a definition by example through the film star's name.

entries.clue: Increase of noise in Great Haywood initially (6)

indicators.note: the noise goes inside the abbreviation for Great
take only the first letter of Haywood

blocks.note: first letter of GT, the abbreviation for Great used in place names
a row is a loud noise, a din
last letter of GT
first letter of Haywood

annotation.surface: A rise in the noise level in Great Haywood, a Staffordshire village.
annotation.walkthrough: Great Haywood is a real English village, so the name reads as one place; but Great splits off as GT, the abbreviation used in names such as Gt Yarmouth.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a rise in size or amount.

entries.clue: Common sense is in the monarch’s domain (7)

blocks.note: first part of REALM, a monarch's kingdom
used as it stands
rest of REALM

annotation.surface: A claim that good sense belongs to the king.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the verb of the sentence, but its letters are the ones placed inside REALM.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a practical, sensible view of how things really are.

entries.clue: Emphasise account needs money (6)

blocks.note: AC (or A/C) is the abbreviation for account
a cent is a coin, a bit of money

annotation.surface: A reminder that a bank account has to have money in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Account' reads as a bank account, but only its abbreviation AC is used.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in its verb sense: to stress a syllable or feature.

entries.clue: Wide awake right after beer (5)

indicators.note: 'after' is about sequence: the word it governs follows the other, so the right goes at the end

blocks.note: ale is a kind of beer
RT is an abbreviation for right

annotation.surface: Someone surprisingly sharp straight after a pint.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface jokes that beer wakes you up; the order is reversed from the clue, with 'right after beer' putting RT at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: watchful and quick to notice.

entries.clue: Very little to track down and find (5)

blocks.note: a tiny, barely detectable amount (noun)
to locate by following clues (verb)

annotation.surface: A complaint that there is hardly anything to go on in a search.
annotation.walkthrough: The first definition is a noun, the second a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Two plain synonyms: a noun for a tiny amount and a verb for following a trail to its end.

entries.clue: Climber’s aid is fiddle around slope (7)

indicators.note: 'around' means surrounding, so the fiddle is wrapped about the slope

blocks.note: first letter of CON, a swindle or fiddle
a ramp is a slope
rest of CON

annotation.surface: A mountaineer's gadget being awkward to handle on a hillside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' in the surface is fiddling around with gear; here it is a con, a swindle.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a spiked plate fixed to a boot to grip ice.

entries.clue: Order international court to stop appointment (7)

indicators.note: the letters plug, or stop up, the middle of DATE

blocks.note: first letter of DATE, an appointment
I is the abbreviation for international
CT is the abbreviation for court
rest of DATE

annotation.surface: A command for an international tribunal to cancel a meeting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stop' in the surface means cancel, but here it means plug a gap, so I and CT fill the inside of DATE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to lay down commands with authority.

entries.clue: What actor must follow Bond’s tech wizard, reportedly (3)

indicators.note: as reported, that is spoken, so a sound-alike

blocks.note: Q is the gadget-maker in the James Bond films

annotation.surface: An actor having to trail behind the gadget man in a Bond film.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface puts the actor on a Bond set, but the letter Q, said out loud, is spelt CUE.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the signal on stage telling an actor when to speak or enter.

entries.clue: Plant, one to come up endlessly (4)

indicators.note: remove the last letter of RISE

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
RISE, to come up, without its last letter

annotation.surface: A gardener's note about a plant that keeps coming up forever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' seems to say the plant never stops coming up, but it means RISE loses its end.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by genus: a flowering garden plant with sword-shaped leaves.

entries.clue: Excessively high prediction of rigged Emirates vote (12)

indicators.note: a rigged vote has been tampered with, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: A suspiciously high forecast of the turnout in a fixed election in the Emirates.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface fits the answer itself: a rigged vote is where you'd expect inflated numbers.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a guess or forecast that comes out too high.
